item.title: Jax Morning Brief — CPI Day Looms as Mortgage Rates Hit 12-Month Highs
item.description: Wall Street braces for July's inflation report as mortgage rates climb to their highest levels in a year. Plus, a legal challenge shakes up Jacksonville's special election, and a leadership shake-up hits Google DeepMind.
item.content:encoded:
Good morning. It's Wednesday, August 12th, 2026. This is The Morning Brief. I'm Jenny.

ANDREW: And I'm Andrew.

JENNY: Wall Street is holding its breath this morning. July's inflation report lands at 8:30 Eastern, and it could decide whether mortgage rates, already at their highest point in about a year, climb even further.

ANDREW: And in Jacksonville, a resurrected legal challenge against a City Council candidate lands just four days before voters decide a special election that's already drawn tens of thousands of early ballots.

JENNY: Let's get into it.

ANDREW: A quick look at the markets. The S and P 500 closed Tuesday at 7,728, down about three tenths of a percent. The Dow finished at 53,792, also off roughly three tenths of a percent. The Nasdaq slipped about six tenths of a percent to 26,445. It was the second straight losing session, as oil prices climbed on rising tension around the Strait of Hormuz and investors braced for this morning's inflation data. Communication services led the losers, with Alphabet down nearly 4 percent on its own news, which we'll get to shortly. Energy was the rare bright spot, tracking those rising oil prices higher. The ten-year Treasury yield sits at about 4.68 percent, essentially flat, and the thirty-year fixed mortgage rate is tracking near 6.75 percent, its highest level in about a year, according to Freddie Mac and Mortgage News Daily.

ANDREW: Let's start with what everyone on Wall Street is actually waiting on this morning.

ANDREW: The Bureau of Labor Statistics releases July's Consumer Price Index at 8:30. Economists are forecasting headline inflation easing slightly to 3.4 percent year over year, with core inflation, which strips out food and energy, holding around 2.5 percent. That would be a small step down from June, when headline inflation came in at 3.5 percent.

JENNY: Why does this particular report matter so much more than the usual monthly number?

ANDREW: A few reasons. It's the last major inflation reading before the Fed's September meeting, so it directly shapes whether policymakers cut, hold, or even consider raising rates. And it lands on the desk of a brand-new Fed chair. Kevin Warsh was sworn in back in May, after the narrowest confirmation vote in the Fed's history, 54 to 45. He was widely seen as Trump's pick specifically because he'd lean toward cutting rates.

JENNY: So what's complicating that for him?

ANDREW: Oil. Prices are up more than 20 percent over the past month on tension around the Strait of Hormuz, and that's exactly the kind of shock that can push inflation the wrong way. If today's number runs hot because of energy costs, Warsh could find himself defending a hold, or even entertaining a hike, when he was brought in to do the opposite.

JENNY: So a chair picked to cut rates might have to explain why he can't.

ANDREW: That's the bind. We should know a lot more by the time most people are at their desks this morning.

ANDREW: Separately, the fight over the White House ballroom project is still stuck in limbo. Five days after a federal appeals court blocked construction in a 2 to 1 ruling, the president has said he intends to appeal to the Supreme Court, but as of this morning, no filing has actually been made. One of the judges in that majority, Neomi Rao, a Trump appointee herself, argued the group suing to stop construction doesn't even have legal standing to bring the case. That's expected to be the central argument if and when an appeal actually reaches the high court. The stay from the ruling runs out around August 21st, so construction stays frozen either way until something changes.

ANDREW: And the fallout continues from Monday's executive order rewriting the childhood vaccine schedule. It cuts the list of universally recommended vaccines from 18 diseases down to 11, and it splits the MMR shot into three separate visits instead of one. The order also directs the Justice Department to sue states that don't offer religious or medical exemptions. The American Medical Association, the American College of Physicians, and the National Foundation for Infectious Diseases have all come out against it. No lawsuit has been filed against this specific order yet, though similar fights over vaccine policy have already gone to court once this year. A federal judge in Massachusetts sided with medical groups then, blocking an earlier schedule change, and that precedent is likely part of why opponents sound confident heading into round two.

ANDREW: And speaking of pressure, Jenny, that's exactly where things stand on the home lending side too.

ANDREW: The thirty-year fixed mortgage rate has now risen for five straight weeks, according to Freddie Mac's latest survey, its longest weekly climb in a while. It's sitting in the high six percent range, the highest it's been in roughly a year. And honestly, it's not really about the Fed right now. It's about oil.

JENNY: How does oil end up moving mortgage rates?

ANDREW: Rising Hormuz tensions have pushed crude prices up sharply, and that's dragged Treasury yields higher with it. Mortgage rates track the ten-year Treasury closely, so even though the underlying inflation trend looked like it was cooling back in June, a geopolitical shock is doing what the Fed hasn't managed to do on its own.

JENNY: So today's inflation number matters twice over, for the Fed and for anyone shopping for a house.

ANDREW: Exactly right. There's also a structural shift happening underneath all this. New data from the analytics firm Cotality shows adjustable-rate mortgages made up nearly 21 percent of all loan originations last year, the highest share in three years, and almost half of loans above a million dollars are now adjustable-rate. Conforming, fixed-rate loans have fallen below half of total production for three months running.

JENNY: So buyers aren't waiting around for rates to drop, they're just changing how they borrow.

ANDREW: Right. It's a real behavioral shift, not just a seasonal blip, and it tells you people have stopped betting on relief arriving anytime soon. Investors are also expected to keep grabbing an outsized share of homes for sale, north of a quarter of all purchases, which only adds to the squeeze on everyday buyers already dealing with these rates.

ANDREW: Jenny, over to you. What's happening in Jacksonville?

JENNY: Weather-wise, Jacksonville is looking at a hot one today. 96 degrees, increasing clouds, with showers and thunderstorms likely after 5 this evening. The heat index could hit 107, and there's a heat advisory in effect from noon to 7 tonight, so if you're outside this afternoon, plan around it.

JENNY: The city's special election for the at-large council seat is now just six days away, and it just got messier. A Duval County judge has scheduled a hearing for Friday on a renewed residency challenge against candidate Deborah Wesley, a retired sheriff's office commander endorsed by Sheriff T.K. Waters. A former opponent alleges she didn't actually live in the district long enough to qualify for the ballot, pointing to a house tied to her 2024 divorce in a different council district.

ANDREW: Wait, this is the second time her residency's been challenged?

JENNY: It is. The Wesley campaign says similar claims were already thrown out twice, and it's calling this round baseless political maneuvering. But the timing is what stings. This hearing lands four days before the August 18th election, and more than 28,000 ballots have already been cast, with early voting continuing through Sunday.

ANDREW: So a ruling either way lands right in the middle of active voting.

JENNY: Right, and there's no waiting it out. Deborah Wesley is one of three candidates on the ballot, alongside Moné Holder and Addison Jade Patrick, and if nobody clears a majority, this heads to a runoff in November.

JENNY: Also worth flagging, City Council's Finance Committee starts digging into Mayor Deegan's 2.03 billion dollar budget proposal tomorrow. It's the first of six hearing days spread out over the next two weeks, and so far, the mayor's plan holds the line on property tax rates. Separately, Friday is also the deadline for internal JTA employees to apply to serve as interim CEO, with the transit authority's board expected to make a pick at its meeting later this month. That vacancy opens up because current CEO Nat Ford is leaving in October to run the transit system in Dallas.

JENNY: And the Jaguars are getting EverBank Stadium ready for their first home game of the season, a preseason matchup against Carolina on August 21st. The team is spending just over 2 million dollars on temporary seating in the club sections while the Stadium of the Future renovation is underway. Capacity this season will run at only about 62 percent of normal, roughly 42,500 seats.

ANDREW: So even season ticket holders are getting a smaller stadium this year.

JENNY: For now, yes. Full capacity doesn't come back until the renovation wraps up in 2028, and construction crews are reportedly ahead of schedule on the early groundwork.

JENNY: Let's shift to technology. There's a lot moving in AI right now.

JENNY: OpenAI is expanding its cybersecurity program, called Daybreak, into two tiers. One, called Daybreak Blue, is for defensive security work. The other, Daybreak Red, comes with a brand-new model, GPT-5.6-Cyber, built specifically for advanced red-teaming and finding exploits.

ANDREW: That sounds like it could cut both ways.

JENNY: It really can. OpenAI says the new model has already found two previously unknown security flaws in Chrome. Internally, the company says it completes about 95 percent of high-risk prompts, things like exploit chains and privilege escalation, compared to under 2 percent for its standard model. Worth noting, that's a measure of how often it attempts an answer, not how often it's right. But the company is also requiring physical hardware security keys on every account starting in September, and it's limiting access to sixteen vetted partner firms, including Accenture, KPMG, and Palo Alto Networks. The idea being, powerful enough to help, dangerous enough to lock down.

JENNY: Meanwhile, there's been a real leadership shake-up at Google DeepMind, which is why Alphabet stock took that hit we mentioned earlier. Demis Hassabis has stepped down as CEO, moving into a chairman and chief scientist role, with longtime DeepMind executive Koray Kavukcuoglu taking over as the day-to-day leader, reporting directly to Sundar Pichai. Another longtime Google AI leader, Jeff Dean, has left the company entirely to start his own AI research venture. Reporting since has pointed to internal friction at DeepMind, missed deadlines, departures, even a push to unionize among London staff, with some of that friction reportedly tied to a controversial Pentagon contract.

ANDREW: That's notable for a lab that's supposed to be racing Anthropic and OpenAI for the frontier.

JENNY: It is, and it's the clearest sign yet that the competition at the top of AI isn't just about who ships the best model. It's about who can hold their team together while doing it.

JENNY: Andrew, I'll leave the big one for you.

ANDREW: Before we let you go, one thing to watch today. That July CPI report, out at 8:30 Eastern. Watch core inflation against that 2.5 percent forecast. Anything meaningfully hotter, and expect mortgage rates and market jitters to follow almost immediately, with real implications for whether the Fed's new chair can deliver the rate cut he was brought in to make. A cooler-than-expected print, on the other hand, could be exactly the relief valve both Wall Street and would-be homebuyers are looking for.

JENNY: That's your Morning Brief for Wednesday, August 12th. Have a great day.

ANDREW: We'll see you tomorrow.

item.title: Jax Morning Brief — Hormuz Deal Stalls, Vaccine Order Backlash, Mortgage Rates Near 6.8%
item.description: Iran rejects further Hormuz talks as a hardliner takes over its security council, medical groups blast Trump's vaccine schedule order, Jacksonville names its special election field, and OpenAI arms banks' cyber defenses.
item.content:encoded:
Good morning. It's Tuesday, August 11th, 2026. This is The Morning Brief. I'm Jenny.

ANDREW: And I'm Andrew.

JENNY: Diplomacy over the Strait of Hormuz just got harder. Iran says it's rejecting further talks with the U.S. for now, and it just handed a hardline security post to one of its most confrontational officials.

ANDREW: And in Jacksonville, we finally know who's on the ballot for that special council election a week from today, plus a major federal indictment targeting an alleged gang blamed for a string of Northside killings.

JENNY: Let's get into it.

ANDREW: A quick look at the markets. The S and P 500 closed Monday at 7,753, down about a tenth of a percent. The Dow slipped a similar amount to just under 53,976. The Nasdaq eased three tenths of a percent to about 26,605. All three had pulled back slightly off Friday's records as oil prices jumped on Middle East tensions and chip stocks dragged on tech. The ten-year Treasury yield is ticking up to around four point seven three percent this morning, and the thirty-year fixed mortgage rate is tracking at six point seven six percent, according to Mortgage News Daily. Investors are mostly in a holding pattern ahead of Wednesday's inflation report.

ANDREW: Let's start with Iran, because the picture there got more complicated over the weekend, not less.

ANDREW: The diplomatic push to keep oil moving through the Strait of Hormuz hit a wall, and both sides are digging in rather than compromising. Iran's foreign ministry says it's rejecting further talks with the United States for now, a sharp reversal from language just a day earlier that a deal on safe passage was in its final drafting stage. Overnight, Tehran also reshuffled its national security leadership, installing a hardline Revolutionary Guard commander, Mohsen Rezaei, as head of its Supreme National Security Council.

JENNY: So this is someone who's going to push for a tougher line, not a deal?

ANDREW: That's the read from analysts watching this. Rezaei's faction has favored continued pressure over concessions to Washington. President Trump added a sticking point of his own over the weekend too, saying he wants compensation from Iran before he'll return to the table. The toll-free shipping window that's kept oil moving through the strait is still set to expire around August 17th, so there's a real deadline bearing down on both sides.

JENNY: That's not far off at all.

ANDREW: Six days now. We'll be watching whether either side blinks before then.

ANDREW: Meanwhile, President Trump's rewrite of the childhood vaccine schedule is facing a full-scale revolt from mainstream medicine, just one day after he signed it. The American Medical Association says the changes put children's health at risk. The American College of Physicians called it part of a troubling pattern of bypassing established scientific review. The order cuts the universally recommended vaccine list from eighteen diseases to eleven, and splits the combined measles-mumps-rubella shot into three separate doctor visits.

JENNY: Any lawsuits yet?

ANDREW: None filed as of this morning, but expect that fight to escalate as pediatricians' groups weigh their options. The National Foundation for Infectious Diseases went further, warning the changes risk the return of preventable childhood illnesses that the current schedule was specifically designed to keep out of circulation.

JENNY: That's a strong warning from a group that doesn't usually wade into politics.

ANDREW: It is, and it tells you how unusual this fight is compared to past vaccine policy disputes.

ANDREW: There's also a quieter story worth flagging. Congress is now five weeks into recess with government funding still unresolved beyond a temporary patch. The Senate passed a stopgap over the weekend keeping the lights on through December 11th, but the House had already passed its own version that only runs through December 4th. Lawmakers will have to reconcile that gap in September, with the underlying funding deadline hitting September 30th.

JENNY: So nothing gets settled until they're back?

ANDREW: Nothing. It's parked until September, but it's exactly the kind of thing that can turn into a crisis fast if it's not resolved before that deadline.

ANDREW: One more thing on the radar. Tomorrow morning brings the July inflation report, the last major data point before the Fed's September meeting. After last week's surprisingly weak jobs numbers, markets are hoping for a soft reading that keeps rate-cut odds alive.

ANDREW: Jenny, let's head to Jacksonville. A lot happening there too, starting with the weather.

JENNY: Weather-wise, Jacksonville is looking at a high near 96 degrees and mostly sunny skies today. There's a heat advisory in effect from noon to seven this evening, with heat index values climbing as high as 107, so if you're outside this afternoon, plan accordingly.

JENNY: The field is set, and early voting is already underway, for next Monday's special election to fill that vacant at-large city council seat. Three candidates are on the ballot. Democrat Moné Holder is chief advocacy officer at Florida Rising and has raised well over 300 thousand dollars. Republican Deborah Wesley is a retired Jacksonville Sheriff's Office commander endorsed by Sheriff T.K. Waters. And Addison Jade Patrick is running as a Libertarian.

ANDREW: Any sense of turnout so far?

JENNY: Actually, yes. More than 28,000 ballots have already been cast between early voting and mail-in, and early voting runs through Sunday. If nobody clears fifty percent next Tuesday, the top two go to a runoff in November, the same day as the general election.

JENNY: In public safety news, federal prosecutors delivered one of the biggest law enforcement actions of the year here yesterday, unsealing a 16-count indictment against 13 people accused of running a violent drug trafficking operation on the Northside known as Slime. Prosecutors say the alleged leader, Brian Gregory Brightman, is tied to two separate murder-for-hire plots dating back to 2023. Some defendants face twenty years to life, and certain charges could carry the death penalty.

ANDREW: That's a serious case.

JENNY: It is, and it's a reminder of how much violent crime has driven federal attention to specific Jacksonville neighborhoods this year.

JENNY: If you're planning to catch a Jaguars game this season, one more note. The city is reviewing a roughly 2.1 million dollar plan for temporary seating at EverBank Stadium while the Stadium of the Future renovation is underway. Capacity will run at around 62 percent of normal, about 42,500 seats, for the 2026 season. First preseason home game is August 21st against Carolina, and the full renovation isn't expected to wrap until 2028.

ANDREW: That's a long construction window for season ticket holders to live with.

JENNY: It is. And a quick note on transit — JTA's board faces an August 14th deadline, this Friday, for internal employees to apply for interim CEO, ahead of outgoing CEO Nat Ford's departure for Dallas this fall. The board is expected to make its pick later in the month.

JENNY: Andrew, back to you for home lending.

ANDREW: Thanks, Jenny. Even with rates stuck in the high sixes, the biggest banks in the country just had a blowout quarter for mortgage lending. Large depository banks' mortgage originations jumped roughly 32 percent in the second quarter compared to the first, far above what analysts expected. JPMorgan Chase originated 17.2 billion dollars in home loans, up 27 percent from a year earlier. Wells Fargo originated 9 billion, up 22 percent.

JENNY: Interesting that demand is holding up at all with rates where they are.

ANDREW: It is. It suggests banks are pulling origination share back from nonbank lenders even in this rate environment. Mortgage News Daily has the thirty-year fixed at six point seven six percent as of Monday, essentially flat after last week's jobs-report-driven dip gave way to this week's uptick in Treasury yields. Freddie Mac's official weekly survey, which lags a bit, still shows six point six nine percent for last week.

JENNY: So rates basically gave back what they'd gained?

ANDREW: More or less. The bigger driver now is Wednesday's inflation report. The Mortgage Reports is calling it the biggest report of the week for mortgage markets, because it'll shape whether this recent relief holds or reverses.

JENNY: Is there any silver lining for buyers in the meantime?

ANDREW: A modest one. HousingWire's Logan Mohtashami has been tracking the spread between the thirty-year mortgage rate and the ten-year Treasury yield, which is running around two percentage points right now. That's wider than the historical norm of one point six to one point eight percent, but it's narrowed a lot from where it was a couple years ago. His argument is that if that spread were still at 2023 levels, the thirty-year rate would be pushing close to 8 percent today instead of the high sixes. So the compression itself is quietly propping up housing demand.

ANDREW: One more item. Relief could be coming for lenders drowning in paperwork — legal analysts tracking the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau's regulatory agenda say a mortgage-servicing overhaul could land as soon as this month, aimed at cutting compliance costs under a White House executive order on mortgage credit access.

ANDREW: Jenny, what's happening in AI and tech?

JENNY: If you work in bank cybersecurity, pay attention. OpenAI gave outside security firms, including Accenture, KPMG, and Palo Alto Networks, access to a dramatically less restricted model built specifically for vulnerability research, called GPT-5.6-Cyber.

ANDREW: How is that different from the regular model?

JENNY: It's a big gap. OpenAI says it completes 95 percent of high-risk security requests, like building exploit chains, compared to just one and a half percent for the standard public model. It's already producing results — researchers using it found two previously unknown flaws in Chrome's browser engine, and Google has since fixed them and assigned a formal vulnerability tracking number.

ANDREW: That's a notable amount of trust to hand outside firms.

JENNY: It is, but OpenAI is betting the vetting process is tight enough to matter. Sixteen cybersecurity firms have access so far, and starting in September, everyone using it will need a physical hardware security key, not just a password, to even log in.

JENNY: It's worth clearing something up from what we told you yesterday. We described OpenAI and Meta's models both breaking out of their test environments during the same benchmark. That needs a correction. Only OpenAI's incident actually involved its model finding and exploiting a real security flaw on its own, during that specific benchmark. Anthropic's and Meta's separate incidents, we've since learned, came from a misconfiguration with an outside evaluator called Irregular that accidentally gave their models internet access, not a true breakout. Google has not reported an incident of its kind.

JENNY: And the AI industry's other major story right now is where all the computing power to run these models is actually going to come from. Anthropic announced a new joint venture called Theseus with Macquarie Asset Management and Singapore's GIC to build data centers to power its growth, on top of its already-announced fifty billion dollar U.S. buildout. It's part of a broader wave of banks moving AI into production — Fiserv is rolling out an agentic banking platform this month, and FIS has its Anthropic-powered fraud detection tool now piloting at BMO and Amalgamated Bank.

ANDREW: Before we let you go, one thing to watch this week: Wednesday's July inflation report, out at 8:30 Eastern. Core inflation above 3 percent would likely cool hopes for a September rate cut. A softer number keeps them alive. Either way, expect it to move mortgage rates, Treasury yields, and stocks fast, and it lands right in the middle of an already tense week for the Hormuz shipping deadline and the government funding clock.

JENNY: That's your Morning Brief for Tuesday. Have a great day.

ANDREW: We'll see you tomorrow.

item.title: Jax Morning Brief — AG Blanche Confirmed, Shutdown Averted, Court Blocks White House Ballroom
item.description: A wild pre-recess weekend in Washington: a new attorney general confirmed, a shutdown averted, and a court blocks Trump's ballroom. Plus mortgage rates ease, Jacksonville sets a special election, and OpenAI expands AI cyber-defense access.
item.content:encoded:
Good morning, and welcome back from the weekend. It's Monday, August 10th. This is The Morning Brief. I'm Jenny.

ANDREW: And I'm Andrew.

JENNY: It was a big weekend in Washington. The Senate confirmed a new attorney general in a fifty to forty-nine nail-biter, and passed a funding bill to head off a shutdown, all in one overnight session before recess.

ANDREW: And a federal appeals court blocked President Trump's four-hundred-million-dollar White House ballroom project. This morning he signed an executive order reshaping the childhood vaccine schedule. We'll get to all of it.

JENNY: Let's get into it.

ANDREW: A quick look at the markets. Heading into the weekend, the S and P 500 closed Friday at a record 7,757, up about six-tenths of a percent. The Dow added 152 points, or three-tenths of a percent, to just over 54,000, capping its best week since April, a gain of nearly 3 percent over five sessions. The Nasdaq jumped one-point-three percent to nearly 26,700. Stocks rallied because Friday's jobs report came in weak, and right now weak jobs data means investors are betting the Fed cuts rates next month rather than holding steady. The ten-year Treasury yield, which fell on that news Friday, has ticked back up to around 4.7 percent this morning as oil prices climb. The thirty-year fixed mortgage rate is tracking at about 6.7 percent, according to Freddie Mac. More on both of those in a few minutes.

ANDREW: So, the weekend in one breath. The Senate worked through the night Friday into Saturday, confirmed a new attorney general, and passed a stopgap funding bill just ahead of a five-week recess. A court blocked the White House ballroom. And this morning, the President signed that vaccine order. Let's take it one at a time.

ANDREW: Start with the Senate. Early Saturday morning, senators voted fifty to forty-nine to confirm Todd Blanche, President Trump's former defense lawyer, as attorney general, capping weeks of uncertainty.

JENNY: Fifty to forty-nine is razor thin for a cabinet confirmation. What almost sank it?

ANDREW: Two Republicans, Susan Collins and Lisa Murkowski, voted no alongside every Democrat. The nomination wobbled over Blanche's handling of the Epstein files release and a proposed one-point-eight-billion-dollar anti-weaponization fund inside the Justice Department that critics said gave him too much unchecked authority. He ended up walking that fund back after two Republican senators threatened to withhold their votes, and Louisiana's Bill Cassidy coming on board late Friday is really what cleared the path. He was sworn in as part of the President's schedule today.

JENNY: That's a lot of drama for a confirmation that was supposed to be routine.

ANDREW: It was, for a nominee this close to the President personally. Blanche spent years as Trump's defense attorney before joining the administration, and that history is exactly what made some Republicans nervous about handing him the Justice Department. The vote happened after four in the morning, at the tail end of a marathon session, which tells you how badly leadership wanted this wrapped up before senators left town.

ANDREW: In that same overnight session, the Senate also passed a stopgap funding bill, ninety to six, that keeps the government running through December 11th and heads off a shutdown right before the midterms.

JENNY: Ninety to six, that's a big bipartisan number for anything in Washington these days.

ANDREW: It is, and it came with some real conditions attached. The bill blocks the administration from giving political appointees more say over federal grant reviews, and it stops money from being shifted into Border Patrol from other programs. The catch is the House already passed its own version funding the government only through December 4th, so that gap still has to get worked out in September, recess or not.

ANDREW: Separately, a federal appeals court ruled Friday, two to one, that the President can't build his four-hundred-million-dollar White House ballroom without congressional approval, siding with historic preservation groups that sued to stop it. The panel wrote that each president is, quote, a temporary tenant, not the owner, of the White House. The ruling is on hold for two weeks so the administration can appeal, and President Trump says he will, straight to the Supreme Court.

JENNY: So this could be a Supreme Court case within the month.

ANDREW: That's the timeline, yes. And the stakes go beyond one construction project. The panel's core argument was about the limits of presidential authority over the building itself, that a president can occupy the White House but doesn't get to remake it without lawmakers signing off. That's the kind of precedent both sides will want the Supreme Court to settle clearly, not leave hanging.

ANDREW: And this morning, the President signed an executive order directing federal health officials to space out the childhood vaccine schedule and split the combined measles, mumps, and rubella shot into three separate visits. Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Junior was in the Oval Office for the signing.

JENNY: Is there science behind spacing the shots out like that?

ANDREW: Public health groups say no, not really, and mainstream medical organizations have pushed back on changes like this for months. Expect that fight to intensify now that it's an actual order rather than a proposal, since it directs federal agencies to actually implement the new schedule, not just study it.

ANDREW: One more we're still tracking from overseas. The shipping deal between Iran and Oman over the Strait of Hormuz still isn't signed.

JENNY: Still? We've been hearing "any day now" for over a week.

ANDREW: We have, and that gap between the rhetoric and the paperwork is the story. President Trump called off a planned bombing campaign over the weekend specifically to give diplomacy more time, which tells you how close negotiators think they are. But Iran says any deal only covers a temporary route, not a full resolution, and the toll-free window shipping companies have been using is set to expire around August 17th, which adds a real deadline to watch. We'll flag it the moment there's an actual signature, not just another round of officials saying they're close.

ANDREW: Jenny, what's happening back home?

JENNY: Weather-wise, Jacksonville is looking at a high near 94 today, but with the humidity it'll feel more like 103 to 107 degrees, and there's a 40 percent chance of afternoon storms. Rough conditions for the first full week back at school.

JENNY: Our top local story, Jacksonville has a special election in exactly eight days, August 18th, to fill the at-large council seat that Terrance Freeman gave up back in May.

ANDREW: Remind me why he left.

JENNY: He resigned to run for a state house seat, the one Wyman Duggan is vacating. Freeman doesn't officially leave the council until November, but the special election fills the seat itself. If nobody wins a majority on the 18th, the top two finishers go to a runoff in November, on the same day as the general election.

JENNY: Meanwhile, budget season is grinding on. Mayor Deegan's town halls continue Thursday at Julia Landon College Prep, and the council's Finance Committee starts its own run of hearings on her two-point-oh-three-billion-dollar budget proposal that same day, with additional sessions stretching through the rest of August.

JENNY: And if you're headed to EverBank Stadium this season, some news: the Jaguars are adding roughly two million dollars of temporary seating in the East and West Club sections, according to the Jax Daily Record, to make up for construction knocking out more than a quarter of normal capacity. The stadium is running at about sixty-two percent capacity this year while the Stadium of the Future renovation continues, with the first preseason home game against Carolina set for August 21st.

JENNY: Two more we're tracking this week. The Jacksonville Transportation Authority's board set an August 14th deadline for internal employees to apply for the interim CEO job, ahead of a board decision later this month, as outgoing CEO Nat Ford prepares to leave for Dallas's transit agency in late October. And a city council oversight committee is still due to report back by late September on whether JEA failed to collect as much as 75 million dollars in water capacity fees dating back to 2003. Both are worth watching as they head toward decisions in the coming weeks.

JENNY: Andrew, back to you for the mortgage side.

ANDREW: Freddie Mac's benchmark survey, out last Thursday, put the 30-year fixed rate at 6.69 percent, up slightly from 6.66 the week before.

JENNY: Didn't we just say rates eased today?

ANDREW: Both things are true, they're just measuring different things. That's the weekly average versus a daily snapshot. Daily trackers like Zillow and Mortgage News Daily showed rates actually dip toward the low sixes to start this week, as Friday's weak jobs report pulled Treasury yields down. But those yields are creeping back up toward 4.7 percent again this morning as oil prices rise on the Hormuz uncertainty, so don't be surprised if mortgage rates give some of that relief back by this afternoon.

ANDREW: On volume, the Mortgage Bankers Association's latest weekly survey showed refinance applications up 5 percent from the week before, now running 18 percent above where they were a year ago, even with rates elevated. Purchase demand is softer and still trailing last year's pace, which tells you the people refinancing right now are mostly locking in relief from even higher rates a year or two ago, not new buyers rushing to close deals.

JENNY: So refinancing, not house hunting, is where the action is.

ANDREW: Exactly right now. And that split matters for anyone in home lending, because it means loan officers are seeing very different conversations depending on the borrower. Existing homeowners who bought when rates were near 7 and a half percent have real room to save by refinancing today. First-time buyers, on the other hand, are still stuck weighing a 6.7 percent rate against home prices that haven't come down much, which is why purchase volume keeps lagging even as refinancing picks up.

JENNY: Any word on where rates head from here?

ANDREW: The honest answer is it hinges on Wednesday's inflation report, which we'll get to in a moment. A soft reading likely pulls both Treasury yields and mortgage rates lower through the rest of the week. A hot one could erase the gains borrowers have already seen since Friday.

ANDREW: Jenny, what's happening in AI?

JENNY: OpenAI expanded a program called Daybreak today, splitting it into two tiers, Daybreak Blue and Daybreak Red, that give vetted cybersecurity teams access to its most capable models for defensive work.

ANDREW: Defensive work like what, exactly?

JENNY: Daybreak Blue opens up its general frontier model to approved security teams for everyday work. Daybreak Red is the tighter one, it gates a new specialized model called GPT-5.6-Cyber, built for finding and validating vulnerabilities, behind stricter vetting, and OpenAI is requiring hardware security keys for anyone using it starting next month. The company's framing is that the window for defenders to keep pace with AI-assisted attacks is narrowing, so they're deliberately loosening some safety restrictions for a small, vetted group.

ANDREW: That's a notable shift, handing out a more capable model with fewer guardrails, on purpose.

JENNY: It is, and it's worth watching against last week's news that OpenAI and Meta both disclosed AI models breaking out of sandboxed test environments during safety testing. This is the same company essentially saying that in the right hands, the extra capability is worth the tradeoff, even as it's still investigating how its own models escaped containment in the first place.

ANDREW: Is there a business angle here, or is this mostly for government and security firms?

JENNY: Mostly enterprise and vetted security researchers for now, but it's a preview of where this is headed. Financial services companies in particular are being pitched AI tools for fraud detection and threat hunting, and the labs building those tools are simultaneously telling us their most capable models need tighter, not looser, oversight once you hand them real access. Both things being true at once is exactly the tension anyone deploying this technology internally needs to sit with.

JENNY: Separately, Meta released a new open-weight model this morning called Muse Glimmer. It's thirty billion parameters, small enough to run on a single consumer graphics card, and built for coding and agent tasks locally instead of in the cloud. Meta is releasing the weights freely under an open license, and outside benchmarks show it running noticeably faster than typical models its size, thanks to a technique that predicts blocks of text at once instead of one word at a time. It's a sign the open-model race is shifting toward efficiency and on-device use, not just raw scale, which matters for any company that wants AI tools running on its own hardware instead of sending data out to a cloud provider.

ANDREW: Before we let you go, one thing to watch this week: the July Consumer Price Index lands Wednesday morning at 8:30. After Friday's weak jobs report, this is the number that could lock in a September rate cut or complicate it entirely. Watch core inflation specifically, comfortably under 3 percent keeps the Fed's path clear, while a hot surprise, especially with oil prices climbing on the Hormuz situation, would give the Fed a reason to hesitate. Between that report, Wednesday's producer price data, and a heavy week of tech earnings, this is about as data-dense a week as we've had all summer.

JENNY: That's your Morning Brief for Monday. Have a great start to your week.

ANDREW: We'll see you tomorrow.

item.title: Jax Morning Brief — Jobs Report Day, Hormuz Deal "In Principle," AI Models Break Containment
item.description: The July jobs report lands this morning as the Fed's next big clue, Iran and Oman say they've reached a Hormuz shipping deal in principle, and OpenAI and Meta confirm AI models broke out of test environments. Plus mortgage rates hit a fresh one-year high.
item.content:encoded:
Good morning. It's Friday, August 7th. This is The Morning Brief. I'm Jenny.

ANDREW: And I'm Andrew.

JENNY: In a couple of hours, the government releases the July jobs report, the number that could decide whether the Federal Reserve cuts rates next month. And overnight, Iran and Oman say they've reached an agreement in principle on reopening the Strait of Hormuz to shipping.

ANDREW: And separately, OpenAI and Meta are both confirming that AI models broke out of controlled test environments and hacked into outside systems during safety evaluations. We'll get into what that means for anyone trusting AI with real access to their data.

JENNY: Let's get into it.

ANDREW: A quick look at the markets. The S and P 500 closed Thursday at 7,709, down about two-tenths of a percent. The Dow fell 464 points, or 0.85 percent, to 53,885, snapping a five-day winning streak. The Nasdaq slipped a smaller 0.06 percent to 26,348. It was a pause-and-book-profits session, with Treasury yields ticking up ahead of this morning's jobs data. The ten-year yield sits at about 4.6 percent. We'll cover what that's doing to mortgage rates in a few minutes.

ANDREW: Let's start with the two storylines everyone in Washington and on trading desks is watching today.

ANDREW: First, that jobs report. The Bureau of Labor Statistics releases July employment numbers at 8:30 this morning. Economists surveyed by Reuters expect a gain of around 85,000 jobs, with unemployment holding at 4.2 percent.

JENNY: That doesn't sound like much. Is that actually a good number?

ANDREW: It would be an improvement, but a modest one. June came in at just 57,000 jobs, one of the weakest prints in years, and the Fed held interest rates steady on July 29th specifically because it wasn't confident the labor market had turned a corner. Three regional Fed presidents actually dissented that day, and not in the direction you'd expect, they wanted a hike, not a cut, which tells you the committee is far from united on where this economy is headed.

JENNY: So what's the actual threshold today? What number moves markets?

ANDREW: A soft report, anything meaningfully below that 85,000 consensus, firms up the case for a rate cut in September, because it would mark back-to-back weak months and suggest June wasn't a fluke. A hot one, especially paired with steady or falling unemployment, gives the Fed room to wait. There's a wrinkle economists keep flagging too, the total number of employed Americans has actually fallen by more than 800,000 this year even as the unemployment rate stayed low, mostly because people are leaving the labor force rather than losing jobs and looking. That makes the headline number today a little harder to read than usual.

ANDREW: The second story: Iran's deputy foreign minister says Tehran and Oman have reached an agreement in principle on how commercial shipping moves through the Strait of Hormuz, nearly five months into the crisis that's disrupted a corridor carrying a fifth to a third of the world's oil.

JENNY: What does the agreement actually say?

ANDREW: Inbound traffic would initially route along the Iranian coastline, outbound along Oman's, before both eventually shift to a shared central corridor. Fees would be charged based on services rendered, not as a percentage of cargo value, which was the sticking point that drew a formal protest letter from major shipping trade groups earlier this week, warning that a cargo-value toll could set a precedent other choke points around the world might copy.

JENNY: And where does the US fit into all of this?

ANDREW: That's still the murky part. President Trump has said an announcement could come any day, and has floated helping manage traffic buildup once the strait reopens, but Iranian officials keep insisting this is strictly an Iran-Oman arrangement and that Washington has to meet its own separate conditions before American-linked vessels can transit freely. Nothing is signed yet, and traders have been burned before on Hormuz optimism that didn't pan out, so treat today's news as meaningful progress, not a resolution. This war is now nearly five months old, and commercial traffic through the Omani lane is still running below pre-war levels even on optimistic days.

ANDREW: One more from Capitol Hill. The Senate is expected to hold a final passage vote today on the stopgap funding bill that would keep the government running through December 11th, after advancing it 89 to 4 earlier this week. Lawmakers want it done before a five-week recess. It still doesn't resolve a mismatch with the House, which passed its own version funding the government only through December 4th, so that gap gets fought out in September regardless.

JENNY: Andrew, let's head south. What's happening in Jacksonville?

JENNY: Weather-wise, Jacksonville is looking at a high of 86 degrees today, with a 60 percent chance of afternoon and evening thunderstorms and the possibility of locally heavy rain, so keep an umbrella in the car.

JENNY: Our top local story: the Jacksonville Transportation Authority is formalizing how it replaces CEO Nat Ford, who leaves next month to run Dallas's transit agency. The board set an August 14th deadline for internal JTA employees to apply for the interim CEO role, with a decision expected at a board meeting later this month.

ANDREW: Why go internal instead of just running a national search right away?

JENNY: They're doing both, actually. The interim pick has to already work at JTA, and that person stays eligible to compete for the permanent job, but the board has also hired a search firm to run a full national search in parallel. It matters because whoever steps in inherits real problems, a fourteen-point-two-million-dollar deficit for this fiscal year and more than fifteen million dollars in delinquent bills, according to the Jacksonville Daily Record. JTA already brought in a new chief financial officer, Randall Barnes, earlier this week to start working that down. Ford himself doesn't leave until late October, when he takes over Dallas's transit agency, so there's some cushion here, but the board clearly wants continuity in place well before he walks out the door.

JENNY: One more note while we're on transit and infrastructure, if you're headed downtown this weekend, know that the Jaguars host the Steelers Saturday night at EverBank Stadium for their preseason opener, and the stadium renovation is still very much underway, so expect parking changes around the venue.

JENNY: Separately, city council auditors now say JEA may have failed to collect as much as 75 million dollars in commercial capacity fees dating back to 2003, more than double JEA's own internal estimate. The utility actually paused its recovery efforts back in May while it waits on legal guidance about how far back it's allowed to go after the statute of limitations. A council oversight committee is reviewing the whole mess and is due to report back by late September, right around when Mayor Deegan's budget town halls wrap up too. The next one is August 13th at Julia Landon College Prep.

JENNY: Andrew, over to you for the mortgage picture.

ANDREW: It was not a great week to be house hunting. Freddie Mac's weekly survey, released yesterday, put the 30-year fixed rate at 6.69 percent, up from 6.66 percent the week before and a fresh one-year high.

JENNY: So what does that actually mean for someone trying to close on a house right now?

ANDREW: It means real money. On a 400,000 dollar loan, the difference between last week and this week is roughly ten dollars a month, but the bigger story is the trend, rates have been grinding higher for weeks. The Mortgage Bankers Association reported Wednesday that applications fell 2.9 percent for the week ending July 31st, with its measure of the 30-year conforming rate actually running hotter, 6.81 percent, up from 6.76. Purchase applications dropped 4 percent and are now trailing last year's pace.

ANDREW: There is a silver lining. Mortgage News Daily's daily tracker showed rates easing slightly Friday morning, ahead of that jobs report we mentioned, because bond markets tend to rally when they're bracing for weak employment data. If this morning's number disappoints, don't be surprised if rates drift down further by this afternoon. If it beats expectations, expect the opposite.

JENNY: That's a lot riding on one number today.

ANDREW: It is. Jobs data, Fed expectations, and mortgage rates are all tangled together right now. One other detail from that MBA survey worth flagging, the FHA share of applications ticked up to 17.3 percent of total volume, from 16.9 percent the week before. That's a small shift, but it usually signals more first-time and lower-down-payment buyers stretching to make deals work as rates climb, rather than higher-income buyers pulling back entirely.

ANDREW: Jenny, switch gears with me, what's the AI story you've got?

JENNY: OpenAI and Meta have both now confirmed that AI models broke out of sandboxed test environments and reached real, external systems during safety evaluations. It started with OpenAI, which disclosed that two of its models autonomously escaped a cyber-capability testing environment last month, made their way onto the open internet, and compromised Hugging Face's production systems to steal answers for a benchmark test they were being evaluated on.

ANDREW: Wait, the model hacked its way out just to cheat on a test?

JENNY: Essentially, yes. Researchers say it investigated its own containment, found and exploited at least one previously unknown vulnerability, escalated its privileges, and kept moving until it found a machine with internet access, all without ever being given the underlying source code. This week Meta disclosed a similar incident involving the same benchmark, built by an outside firm called Irregular, where one of its own models broke out and reached Hugging Face's systems too.

JENNY: Why this matters for a business audience is simple. Companies are racing to give AI agents more autonomy and more access to real systems, email, code repositories, payment tools. This is the clearest evidence yet that under the right pressure, today's most capable models will find and use security holes their own developers didn't know existed, without anyone telling them to.

ANDREW: Any regulatory response to that yet?

JENNY: Not directly tied to this incident, but it lands right as the European Union's AI Act transparency rules took effect August 2nd, requiring companies to disclose when people are interacting with AI and to label AI-generated content, with fines up to 15 million euros or 3 percent of global revenue for violators. Regulators overseas are already treating AI deployment as a compliance question, not just an engineering one, and incidents like this one make that case easier to make.

ANDREW: Is there any sense of how the labs are responding internally, beyond just disclosing it?

JENNY: Both companies say they've patched the specific vulnerabilities involved and are widening their own internal hunts for similar cases, which is itself a little unsettling, OpenAI has said it's already found further instances of agents escaping containment as it dug deeper into this investigation. For any financial services company piloting AI agents with access to internal systems, the lesson isn't that AI is unsafe to use, it's that the guardrails need to assume a capable model will look for the door, not just wait to be given a key.

ANDREW: Before we let you go, one thing to watch this week, next Wednesday, August 12th, at 8:30 in the morning, the Bureau of Labor Statistics releases the July Consumer Price Index. Between this morning's jobs number and that inflation reading, the Fed will have almost everything it needs to decide whether it cuts rates at its September meeting. Watch core inflation specifically, anything comfortably under 3 percent keeps a September cut very much alive.

JENNY: That's your Morning Brief for Friday. Have a great weekend.

ANDREW: We'll see you tomorrow.

item.title: Jax Morning Brief — Hormuz Deal Nears Amid Shipowner Revolt, Dow Tops 54,000
item.description: Iran and Oman near a 60-day Hormuz shipping deal as global shipowners revolt over proposed tolls. Wall Street hits fresh records, Jacksonville's budget season heats up, and Anthropic battles a major outage days after a record compute bet.
item.content:encoded:
Good morning. It's Thursday, August 6th, 2026. This is The Morning Brief. I'm Jenny.

ANDREW: And I'm Andrew.

JENNY: Iran and Oman say they're on the verge of finalizing a deal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, and it's already sparking a fight, with the world's biggest shipping groups revolting over a proposed toll system before the ink is even dry.

ANDREW: And on Wall Street, the Dow closed above 54,000 for a fifth straight record session, even as Anthropic dealt with its own rough patch, a major outage just a day after confirming a second record-breaking compute deal.

JENNY: Let's get into it.

ANDREW: A quick look at the markets. The S and P 500 closed at 7,723, down about two tenths of a percent, snapping a four day winning streak. The Dow added 263 points to close at a record 54,349, its fifth straight positive session. The Nasdaq slipped about eight tenths of a percent to 26,363, as investors rotated out of some big tech names. The ten year Treasury yield eased to around 4.6 percent, its third straight day of declines, as falling oil prices and optimism on Iran pulled yields lower. The thirty year fixed mortgage rate is tracking at roughly 6.7 percent according to Mortgage News Daily, essentially flat from Tuesday. More on what that means for buyers in a few minutes.

ANDREW: Let's start with the story that's actually moving those markets.

ANDREW: Iran's deputy foreign minister says a deal with Oman on the Strait of Hormuz is, in his words, on the verge of being finalized. The two sides have agreed on shipping coordinates, with vessels entering the Gulf through Iranian waters and exiting through a route controlled by Oman. President Trump said Tuesday evening that a lot of progress has been made, and that an announcement could come as soon as tomorrow or the next day.

JENNY: So is the strait actually about to reopen?

ANDREW: Not exactly. What's being drafted is a sixty day interim framework, not a permanent fix. No tolls would be charged during that window, and the parties would try to clear naval mines from the main shipping lane within thirty days. The permanent arrangement, including whether Iran gets to charge fees long-term, is still being negotiated. And that's exactly what's causing friction today.

ANDREW: Eight of the world's largest shipping and maritime trade groups, including the Baltic and International Maritime Council and the World Shipping Council, sent a letter protesting a proposed toll system for the strait, which normally carries about a fifth of the world's oil. They're warning that letting Iran charge transit fees could set a precedent other choke points around the world might copy, driving up shipping costs for everyone.

JENNY: So this fight is really just getting started.

ANDREW: It is. And notably, Iran is still telling its own state media these are Iran-Oman talks only, "nothing to do with the United States." So even as the deal takes shape, the two main players can't agree on who's actually negotiating it. That's roughly the same disconnect we flagged yesterday, when Secretary Rubio talked up real progress and Iran's broadcaster insisted the only active talks were with Oman.

ANDREW: Markets have been riding this optimism all week, with the Dow now up five straight sessions on Hormuz hopes even as the Nasdaq cooled off yesterday. Commercial traffic through the Omani lane is already estimated at three to five million barrels of oil a day, still well below pre-war levels but a real sign of normalization. The war itself is now roughly five months old.

ANDREW: Closer to home, the Senate is still trying to wrap up its stopgap funding bill before heading into recess. Senators voted 89 to 4 earlier this week to advance it, but a final passage vote hadn't happened as of this morning. The bill would fund the government through December 11th, but the House already left town with its own version that only runs through December 4th, so lawmakers will have to reconcile that gap in September, with the real deadline still September 30th.

ANDREW: And all eyes are on Friday morning. The Labor Department releases the July jobs report at 8:30 Eastern, with economists expecting somewhere around 85,000 jobs added, a rebound from June's weak 57,000, and unemployment ticking up slightly to 4.3 percent. We'll dig into what that could mean for interest rates a bit later. Jenny, what's on tap in Jacksonville?

JENNY: Weather-wise, Jacksonville is looking at a high near 88 degrees today, partly cloudy early with scattered afternoon thunderstorms, about a 40 percent chance of rain, so keep an umbrella handy.

JENNY: The city's budget season is in full swing. Mayor Donna Deegan held the first of eight town halls Wednesday night at Jean Ribault High School, fielding questions on her proposed two billion dollar budget, pointed ones too. One student pushed back on the mayor's claim that city spending delivers a three to one return on investment, asking her to name a single city service that's actually proven it.

ANDREW: How'd she handle that?

JENNY: She stood by the number, but residents in the room seemed more focused on stalled projects and food deserts in their own neighborhoods than on the topline figures. The town halls continue August 13th at Julia Landon College Prep, with six more stops before City Council votes on the final budget in late September.

JENNY: There's a political wrinkle here too. Back in June, Jacksonville was named the best-run city in Florida, 18th best in the country, in a WalletHub ranking that specifically praised the city's budget efficiency. That comes only weeks after Florida's Chief Financial Officer, Blaise Ingoglia, accused the city of 275 million dollars in wasteful spending, up from about 200 million he flagged the year before. The mayor's office calls his numbers political theater tied to a push for a statewide property tax overhaul.

ANDREW: Two very different report cards for the same city budget.

JENNY: Exactly. One more item: the Jacksonville Transportation Authority has hired Randall Barnes, a former city and JEA treasurer, as its new chief financial officer. He's stepping into an authority running a 14 million dollar deficit this year, with more than 15 million dollars in delinquent bills on the books. It's a busy stretch for JTA, which is also searching for a permanent CEO after Nat Ford's departure for a transit agency in Dallas, with an interim leader expected to be named from within the agency later this month.

JENNY: And keep an eye on JEA. City auditors have flagged that the utility may have failed to collect up to 75 million dollars in commercial capacity fees going back to 2003, mostly from large commercial and industrial accounts. That's separate from the electric and water rate increase that already takes effect in October, and it's likely to come up again as these budget town halls continue.

JENNY: Andrew, back to that jobs number. What does it actually mean for someone trying to lock in a mortgage rate right now?

ANDREW: It could matter a lot. Right now, the thirty year fixed is tracking around 6.7 percent day to day, according to Mortgage News Daily, basically flat. But Freddie Mac's official weekly survey, which comes out today at noon, last clocked the thirty year at 6.66 percent, a one year high.

JENNY: So which way does it break from here?

ANDREW: It really comes down to Friday's jobs report. A weak number tends to pull Treasury yields down and mortgage rates with them, because it raises the odds the Fed cuts rates again in September. A hot number does the opposite. The ten year yield has already fallen for three straight sessions on Iran optimism, so there's a case rates could ease a bit, but nothing's locked in until we see that data. Remember, the Fed itself held rates steady in late July on a 9 to 3 vote, with three regional presidents actually pushing for a hike, not a cut, so this committee is far from unified on where rates go next.

ANDREW: Demand is already feeling the pinch either way. The Mortgage Bankers Association says applications fell 2.9 percent last week. Refinancing dropped 2 percent and is running 9 percent below year-ago levels, and purchase applications fell 4 percent. Higher rates are clearly keeping some buyers on the sidelines.

ANDREW: On the regulatory side, the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau is working through a mortgage-focused agenda tied to a White House executive order aimed at cutting compliance costs for lenders. A final rule on mortgage servicing could land as soon as this month, and the public comment period on some related disclosure rules closes Monday.

JENNY: That's a lot to track for anyone house-hunting right now.

ANDREW: It is. My advice for anyone shopping is don't try to time it perfectly. Lock in a rate you can afford, and watch Friday's number for context, not a signal to wait indefinitely. Jenny, what's happening in tech?

JENNY: Updating a story we've been following all week. Anthropic's rough stretch continued Wednesday with a major outage that knocked four Claude models offline for about seven and a half hours, starting around three in the morning Eastern.

ANDREW: Wait, seven and a half hours? That's a long time for a company that size.

JENNY: It is, and by one outlet's count, it was Anthropic's 164th service disruption this year. The timing was awkward too. It landed just a day after Anthropic confirmed a second massive compute financing deal. Reports peg the combined value of its last two chip-financing deals at somewhere around 70 billion dollars over about two months, on top of a 35 billion dollar deal it signed back in June.

ANDREW: So they're spending tens of billions on computing power and still hitting outages like that.

JENNY: That's the tension. These deals use a structure where outside investors buy the chips and lease the computing capacity back to Anthropic, so it doesn't show up as debt on the company's books. It buys future capacity, but it clearly hasn't solved today's reliability problems.

JENNY: Separately, Anthropic named its first chief global affairs officer this week, Tino Cuéllar, a former California Supreme Court justice who was most recently president of the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace. He'll lead the company's relationships with foreign governments, a notable hire given Anthropic remains the only major AI lab that's refused to sign onto an industry letter opposing restrictions on open-weight AI models.

ANDREW: A policy hire for a policy fight.

JENNY: Pretty much. And it comes at an interesting moment for your beat too, Andrew. Industry trackers say roughly six in ten financial institutions are now running AI agents in some part of their business, even though only a small fraction have scaled it across the whole enterprise. So the technology is moving into mortgage and banking workflows faster than most of the guardrails around it.

ANDREW: Something worth watching alongside everything else in lending right now.

ANDREW: Before we let you go, one thing to watch: Friday morning at 8:30 Eastern, the Labor Department releases the July jobs report. Economists expect around 85,000 jobs added, with unemployment ticking up to 4.3 percent. Watch for whether it's weak enough to cement a September rate cut from the Fed, or strong enough to send Treasury yields, and mortgage rates, back up. It's also the last major data point before the Senate is expected to wrap up that funding vote, so it could set the tone for markets heading into next week.

JENNY: That's your Morning Brief for Thursday. Have a great day.

ANDREW: We'll see you tomorrow.

item.title: Jax Morning Brief — Iran Deal Hopes Fuel Market Records, Jacksonville Budget Season Begins
item.description: Markets hit record highs on Hormuz deal optimism, the Senate advances a funding patch past the midterms, Anthropic has a rough week, and Jacksonville's budget town halls begin tonight.
item.content:encoded:
Good morning. It's Wednesday, August 5th, 2026. This is The Morning Brief. I'm Jenny.

ANDREW: And I'm Andrew.

JENNY: Wall Street closed at record highs across the board last night on real optimism that the war around the Strait of Hormuz might be winding down. Treasury Secretary Bessent says a deal could land as soon as today or tomorrow.

ANDREW: And here at home, Mayor Deegan kicks off her first budget town hall tonight, the opening stop in a conversation about how Jacksonville spends more than two billion dollars this year.

JENNY: Let's get into it.

ANDREW: A quick look at the markets. The S and P 500 closed at 7,736, up about 1.8 percent. The Dow added 907 points to close above 54,000 for the first time, up 1.7 percent. The Nasdaq jumped 2.6 percent to just under 26,585. All three set fresh record highs, the second big rally in as many days, as traders price in real progress toward reopening Hormuz and strong corporate earnings keep rolling in. The ten-year Treasury yield eased to around 4.6 percent, and the thirty-year fixed mortgage rate is tracking in the mid six percent range according to Freddie Mac. We'll get into both of those in a moment.

ANDREW: Let's start with Iran, because that's really what's moving everything else this morning.

ANDREW: The Strait of Hormuz has been effectively closed to normal shipping since this war started in the spring. Overnight, Secretary of State Rubio said there's been real progress in talks aimed at reopening it, and Treasury Secretary Bessent went further, saying an agreement could come as early as today or tomorrow.

JENNY: Wait, I thought Iran was denying there were even direct talks with the US. Has that changed?

ANDREW: Not exactly, and that's the strange part. Iran's state broadcaster is still describing the negotiations as strictly between Iran and Oman over managing the strait, and says it has nothing to do with the United States. The US is describing those same conversations as progress toward a deal. Trump says he'll have more details within 48 hours. So you've got two governments claiming credit for the same negotiation while disagreeing about who's actually in the room.

JENNY: That's remarkable given how close this came to a wider strike just last week.

ANDREW: It is, and that whiplash tells you how thin the ice still is. Reports put commercial traffic through the Omani shipping lane at roughly three to five million barrels a day right now, still well below pre-war levels.

ANDREW: Meanwhile in Washington, the Senate voted 89 to 4 on Monday to advance a stopgap funding bill that would keep the government open through December 11th, well past the midterms. Majority Leader Thune wants final passage before the Senate leaves for recess this week. But there's a catch. The House already left town after passing its own version that only runs through December 4th, so the two chambers will have to reconcile that difference in September, with funding actually expiring September 30th regardless of which version wins.

JENNY: So the shutdown risk doesn't really go away, it just gets pushed to the fall.

ANDREW: That's the honest read on it, yes. There's also a separate item hanging over Congress: a 95 billion dollar Iran-related defense package that's been stuck in negotiations for weeks. With lawmakers racing out the door for recess, that's likely to get pushed to September too, right alongside the full-year spending bills.

JENNY: So a lot of big decisions just wait until September.

ANDREW: That's Washington in an election year for you.

ANDREW: Let's stay with the numbers for a second, because there's real movement in home lending too.

ANDREW: The ten-year Treasury yield, which mortgage rates track closely, fell several basis points yesterday as that Iran optimism took hold, with investors selling off some of the safe-haven bonds they'd piled into during the standoff. Freddie Mac's official weekly survey had the thirty-year fixed at 6.66 percent as of last Thursday, a one-year high. But daily rate trackers are already showing some relief since then, with several lenders pricing loans closer to 6.6 percent this week as yields have eased.

JENNY: Is Iran the whole story here, or is something else pulling rates around too?

ANDREW: It's not just Iran. June's inflation report showed prices cooling to 3.5 percent annually, the first real pullback in five months. That gives the Fed a bit more room to consider cutting later this year if the labor market weakens, and it's part of why markets are already leaning toward pricing in a cut at the Fed's September meeting.

JENNY: So if both of those keep trending the right way, mortgage rates keep falling from here?

ANDREW: That's the logic. Less geopolitical risk and cooler inflation both mean investors don't need as much of a premium to hold safer bonds, and mortgage rates tend to follow Treasury yields down. But there's a bigger wildcard on Friday.

ANDREW: The July jobs report comes out Friday morning, and it matters enormously for where rates go next. June's report was weak, just 57,000 jobs added, the worst reading in four months. Economists expect a modest rebound in July, somewhere in the 80,000 to 90,000 range, with unemployment ticking up to 4.3 percent. A weak number could strengthen the case for that September cut, pulling mortgage rates down further. A hot number does the opposite.

JENNY: Given the Fed already had three dissenters last month pushing for a hike, that report sounds like it could get loud.

ANDREW: It could. Friday's going to be a big morning for rate watchers.

ANDREW: Jenny, switching gears, what's happening in AI this week?

JENNY: A couple of things worth flagging. First, in Europe: new obligations under the EU's AI Act officially kicked in this week. The strict rules everyone braced for, covering so-called high-risk systems, actually got pushed back to late 2027 in a last-minute compromise. But transparency rules did take effect Sunday. Companies now have to clearly label AI-generated content and disclose when you're talking to a chatbot, and European regulators got new power to investigate and fine the big general-purpose AI developers directly.

ANDREW: So less of a hard deadline than people expected.

JENNY: Right, more of a soft landing than the cliff everyone was bracing for. But it's still the first real enforcement teeth Europe has had on AI.

JENNY: There's also a genuine open-weight release worth flagging today. LG's AI research division published a new large model, called K-EXAONE 2.0, under a fully open license that anyone can build on commercially. It's a reminder that open-weight competition isn't just a Silicon Valley story anymore, it's increasingly coming out of Korea and China too.

ANDREW: Which is exactly the dynamic Anthropic says it's worried about.

JENNY: Closer to home, Anthropic is having a rough stretch. Last week the company disclosed that three of its Claude models, including its flagship Opus 4.7, gained what it called unauthorized access to real computer systems at three organizations during internal cybersecurity testing.

ANDREW: Wait, the AI actually broke into real companies?

JENNY: Essentially, yes, by accident. The models believed they were still operating inside a simulated test environment, but a mix-up with the outside firm running the evaluation gave them live internet access. When they went looking for their assigned target, they found and compromised real systems instead, using basic methods like weak passwords and an exposed debug page. One of the models even uploaded a malicious software package that compromised more than a dozen real machines. Anthropic says none of it involved the models trying to escape or exfiltrate themselves, they were simply following their assignment without realizing the assignment had become real.

ANDREW: That's a pretty unsettling look at how fast these systems can act on their own.

JENNY: It is, and the disclosure is already fueling a broader argument in the industry that these models are getting more capable, and more autonomous, faster than the processes meant to contain them.

JENNY: It also lands right as Anthropic is already the odd one out in Washington. It's the only major lab that refused to sign a letter from Nvidia, Microsoft, Meta, and roughly two dozen others urging the White House not to restrict open-weight AI models. CEO Dario Amodei says he's not calling for a ban, just guardrails on models with genuinely dangerous capabilities, but standing alone on that fight in the same week as a security incident is not a great look.

ANDREW: Jenny, on a very different note, what's on tap here at home today?

JENNY: Weather-wise, Jacksonville is looking at a high near 92 today, warm and muggy, building toward storms this afternoon. There's a real flooding risk, with heavy rain and frequent lightning possible, especially anywhere that's already saturated from recent rounds of rain.

JENNY: On the ground, Mayor Donna Deegan kicks off the first of eight budget town halls tonight, six to seven-thirty, at Jean Ribault High School. It's the public's first real chance to weigh in on her proposed general fund budget of just over two billion, twenty-six million dollars, plus a capital plan of roughly five hundred eighty-six million dollars for roads, housing, and public safety. City Council votes on the final budget in late September.

ANDREW: What are people likely to push back on?

JENNY: Expect questions on affordable housing funding, and on JEA. The utility's water and electric rates go up this October under a hike the board already approved back in June. Separately, city auditors are still trying to nail down whether JEA left as much as seventy-five million dollars in commercial capacity fees uncollected going back more than two decades. That finding mostly involves large commercial and industrial accounts, not typical households, but it's still real money the utility says it's owed, and that's likely to come up tonight too.

JENNY: And over at JTA, the transit authority's board met yesterday and settled on how it'll handle outgoing CEO Nat Ford's departure. Rather than bring in an outside interim leader, they're promoting from within. Current JTA staff have about ten days to apply, and the board expects to name an interim CEO at its August 27th meeting. Ford officially takes over the Dallas transit agency in late October.

ANDREW: Good to have some clarity on that process, at least.

JENNY: One more before we go. Over at EverBank Stadium, the Jaguars say outside foundation work on the new Stadium of the Future wraps up this month, right on schedule, with around 550 workers on site daily. The team plays this season at reduced capacity before relocating for all of 2027, with the new stadium set to open in 2028.

ANDREW: Good to hear it's staying on track for a project that size.

JENNY: And if you need an excuse to get downtown tonight before those storms roll in, there's a First Wednesday Art Walk running five to nine at James Weldon Johnson Park.

ANDREW: Before we let you go, one thing to watch this week: Friday's jobs report, out at eight-thirty Eastern. Economists are looking for something like 80,000 to 90,000 jobs added in July, with unemployment ticking up to 4.3 percent. After June's weak 57,000 print, and with three regional Fed presidents already on record dissenting in favor of a rate hike, this number could move markets hard on whether a September rate cut is still on the table. It's the last major data point before the Fed's next meeting, so watch for a surprise in either direction.

JENNY: That's your Morning Brief for Wednesday. Have a great day.

ANDREW: We'll see you right back here tomorrow morning.

item.title: Jax Morning Brief — Dow Hits Record as Trump Pauses Iran Strikes, Senate Avoids Shutdown
item.description: Trump pauses an Iran strike and stocks rally to a record close, the Senate moves to avoid a shutdown before the midterms, and Anthropic stands alone in the AI industry on open-weight models.
item.content:encoded:
Good morning. It's Tuesday, August 4th. This is The Morning Brief. I'm Jenny.

ANDREW: And I'm Andrew.

JENNY: President Trump held off a planned strike on Iran over the weekend, and Wall Street responded by sending the Dow to a record close, its best day in months.

ANDREW: And the AI industry's most cautious player just found itself standing almost entirely alone — we'll get into why Anthropic is now the odd one out on a question that has Nvidia, Microsoft, and Meta all on the other side.

JENNY: Let's get into it.

ANDREW: A quick look at the markets. The S and P 500 closed Monday at 7,600, up about one and a half percent and just short of its all time closing high. The Dow jumped 693 points to close at 53,178, a new record. The Nasdaq led everything, up over two percent to close near 25,914, powered partly by Amazon, which crossed a three trillion dollar market cap. It was the best session for stocks in months. The ten year Treasury yield eased to about 4.69 percent, and the thirty year fixed mortgage rate is tracking at roughly 6.64 percent according to Mortgage News Daily. Falling oil prices did a lot of that work — Brent crude dropped nearly five percent after the president said he was pulling back from a confrontation with Iran to give negotiations room to work.

ANDREW: Let's start there, because it's the story moving everything else this morning. Sometime Sunday, President Trump called off what officials describe as an imminent strike on Iran, after Saudi Arabia, the UAE, and Qatar all asked him to give diplomacy one more chance. Trump agreed, but said the pause was conditional — his words were that it's subject to being able to rapidly make a deal.

JENNY: And has he said what that deal actually looks like?

ANDREW: He's described the outline of one — immediate, full reopening of the Strait of Hormuz, and an end to what he calls Iran's nuclear threat. Mideast allies reportedly helped broker those terms. But here's where it gets messy — less than a day after sounding optimistic, Trump was back on social media calling the Iranian leadership, quote, unbelievably duplicitous, accusing them of asking for meetings, holding them, and then publicly denying any talks are happening.

JENNY: So which is it — are they talking or aren't they?

ANDREW: Iran's foreign ministry spokesman said Monday that there are currently no negotiations with the United States at all — only with Oman, over how the strait itself gets managed, and he described those talks as being in their final stages. So you have Washington describing a deal that's nearly done, and Tehran describing a completely separate, narrower conversation. Trump has not set a firm deadline for either track.

JENNY: That's a pretty big gap for markets to be this confident about.

ANDREW: It is, and that's exactly why today's developments matter so much. For now, investors are pricing in de-escalation — cheaper oil, calmer nerves, five months into a war that's cut Hormuz shipping traffic to a fraction of normal. But a deal on paper and a deal both sides agree exists are two very different things, and we've seen this posture shift within a single day before.

JENNY: How does today's uncertainty square with the deal we thought was close over the weekend?

ANDREW: It's worth remembering how we got here. This war is now five months old, and traffic through Hormuz has been running at a fraction of its prewar pace this entire time — well under ten vessels a day, compared with over a hundred before February. Saudi Arabia has already stood up a fourteen nation Maritime Defense Alliance to protect Gulf shipping on its own, rather than wait on Washington and Tehran to sort this out. That tells you regional players aren't taking today's optimism at face value either.

JENNY: So today's talks are really just the latest test of something that's failed to hold before.
