ANDREW: Exactly, and that's the lens to watch this through — not as a fresh start, but as another attempt at a resolution that's slipped through everyone's hands more than once already.

ANDREW: The other big move out of Washington: Senate leaders unveiled a short-term spending bill Monday that would fund the federal government at current levels through December 11th, well past the midterm elections. Majority Leader Thune called it his top priority before the chamber leaves for August recess, telling colleagues plainly that the country cannot afford a third shutdown this year. Democrats, including Minority Leader Schumer, appear to be softening their opposition enough to let it move.

JENNY: Any sense of whether it actually gets a vote before recess?

ANDREW: That's the open question, and it's one we'll flag again before we go. Congress still hasn't finished the dozen individual spending bills that actually fund the government long-term, so this is a bridge, not a resolution — just enough to keep the lights on through the election season. It's also notable that this bill exists at all, given the same chamber couldn't find the votes last week for a separate ninety five billion dollar package tied to defense spending around the Iran conflict — that effort may now get punted to September entirely.

JENNY: Andrew, since rates are already moving on all this Iran news, what's the mortgage picture looking like?

ANDREW: Mostly steady, which itself is a little surprising. Mortgage News Daily has the thirty year fixed at about 6.64 percent this morning, down just a hair from yesterday. That's essentially flat with where Freddie Mac's official weekly survey put it last Thursday, at 6.66 percent — a one year high we told you about Monday.

JENNY: So all that market drama isn't actually moving the rate buyers see?

ANDREW: Not yet, and here's why — mortgage rates track the ten year Treasury more than they track the stock market, and that yield only eased slightly, from 4.74 percent Friday to 4.69 percent now. Lower oil prices help the inflation outlook at the margins, which is good for rates long term, but it's a small move, not a turning point. Freddie Mac's next weekly survey comes out Thursday, and that will tell us whether this is the start of a real pullback or just noise.

JENNY: Given three Fed officials just voted for a hike instead of a hold, I'd guess you're not expecting a big drop.

ANDREW: I wouldn't bet on one. With inflation risk still very much alive in that Fed debate, and Friday's jobs report still to come, buyers shouldn't expect meaningful relief just because oil had one good day.

ANDREW: Jenny, over to you — what's happening in AI this morning?

JENNY: The story with real staying power is Anthropic finding itself increasingly isolated within its own industry. Roughly two dozen tech companies — led by Nvidia, Microsoft, and Meta — sent a letter to the White House last week urging against what they called premature restrictions on open-weight AI models, the kind anyone can download and run themselves. Anthropic is the most prominent holdout, refusing to sign.

ANDREW: What's Anthropic's actual objection — do they think open models are dangerous, full stop?

JENNY: Not quite, according to CEO Dario Amodei, who pushed back this week on the idea that Anthropic wants a blanket ban. He says open-weight models are, in his words, a public good, as long as they don't carry genuinely dangerous capabilities — things like helping someone build a weapon. But that distinction hasn't stopped nearly the entire rest of the industry from lining up against him on the policy question.

ANDREW: That's a striking position for the company that's supposed to be everyone's safety-conscious peer.

JENNY: It is, and it's not happening in a vacuum — this ties back to what we told you last week about Moonshot AI's Kimi K3 release out of China, which the White House has separately accused of being built in part on stolen American research. Anthropic's argument is that loosening the rules now hands China's labs an even bigger head start. Critics say Anthropic is just protecting its own competitive position while everyone else races ahead on cheaper, open alternatives.

ANDREW: Is there a real business risk here, or is this mostly a policy fight playing out in public?

JENNY: There's a real business angle too. Anthropic just became the world's most valuable AI startup, and part of how it got there is by positioning itself as the safety-first alternative to everyone else. Taking the lonely position on open weights reinforces that brand, but it also means Anthropic is now negotiating alone against a coalition that includes some of its own cloud and chip partners — not a comfortable spot for a company that still depends on those relationships.

JENNY: In smaller AI news, OpenAI is retiring its original DALL-E image tool inside ChatGPT at the end of this month, pushing everyone toward its newer ChatGPT Images feature instead — a housekeeping move, but a reminder of how fast even flagship products get replaced in this industry right now.

ANDREW: Jenny, let's get you home — what's the latest in Jacksonville?

JENNY: Weather-wise, expect a high near 90 degrees today with scattered afternoon storms likely, so plan around the rain if you're out this afternoon.

ANDREW: What's the big local story today?

JENNY: Jacksonville's transit authority took a real step forward in replacing its longtime chief. The JTA board's new CEO selection committee — all seven board members — held its first meeting today, kicking off the formal search to replace Nat Ford, who's leaving to run Dallas's transit system starting in October. The timeline calls for accepting applications through the fall, interviews after that, and a final decision by December.

ANDREW: That's a long runway. Who's actually running JTA in the meantime?

JENNY: That's still being sorted out, and it's one of the bigger open questions the committee has to answer early — Ford's departure date is fast approaching, and the board has already signaled it wants a search firm involved rather than handling this alone, though it hasn't hired one yet.

ANDREW: Anything else on the local calendar this week?

JENNY: Yes — Mayor Deegan kicks off her budget town hall series tomorrow night at Jean Ribault High School, the first of eight stops where residents can weigh in on her 2.03 billion dollar spending plan before Council votes this fall. It's a good chance for anyone with questions about public safety or infrastructure spending to actually ask them directly.

ANDREW: Sounds like a busy back half of the week for city government.

JENNY: It is, and JEA is quietly working through its own decision in the background — the utility is still weighing whether to raise rates as soon as October, as its board continues sorting out a fee-collection shortfall that auditors say could total as much as seventy five million dollars going back over two decades. No vote yet, but it's one more thing likely to come up when residents pack that gym tomorrow night.

ANDREW: Given how much else is on that budget agenda, I imagine JEA rates will be one of the first questions asked.

JENNY: I'd bet on it.

ANDREW: Before we let you go, one thing to watch this week: whether the Senate actually passes that stopgap funding bill before lawmakers leave for August recess at week's end. If it slips, the shutdown risk we just told you about resurfaces right as campaign season heats up. And keep Friday on your radar too — the July jobs report lands at eight thirty Eastern, and after three Fed officials just voted for a hike instead of a hold, a hot number could hand them real ammunition heading into September.

JENNY: That's your Morning Brief for Tuesday. Have a great day.

ANDREW: We'll see you tomorrow.
